content: Stool softeners are medications prescribed for short-term use to alleviate constipation. They are particularly recommended for individuals who need to avoid straining during bowel movements due to conditions such as heart problems, hemorrhoids, or other medical issues. These medications work by softening the stool, making it easier to pass. In some cases, stool softeners may be prescribed for other purposes; consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information. Stool softeners are available in various forms, including capsules, tablets, liquids, and syrups, all of which are taken orally. Typically, they are taken at bedtime. It is important to follow the instructions provided on the packaging or prescription label carefully. If you have any questions or concerns, ask your doctor or pharmacist for clarification. Take the medication exactly as directed, without exceeding or reducing the prescribed dose or frequency. Capsules and tablets should be swallowed with a full glass of water. The liquid form is supplied with a specially marked dropper for accurate dosing; if you have trouble using it, ask your pharmacist for guidance. To mask the bitter taste of the liquid (not the syrup), mix it with 4 ounces of milk, fruit juice, or formula. Stool softeners generally take one to three days of consistent use to produce an effect. Do not use stool softeners for more than one week unless instructed otherwise by your doctor. If you experience sudden changes in bowel habits lasting more than two weeks or if your stools remain hard after one week of use, contact your doctor. Before using stool softeners, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you have any allergies to medications. Additionally, provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications you are currently taking, especially aspirin and vitamins. Do not take mineral oil while using stool softeners. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, notify your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking stool softeners, consult your doctor immediately. If you forget to take a dose, this medication is usually taken as needed. However, if your doctor has instructed you to take it regularly, take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular dosing schedule. Do not take a double dose to compensate for a missed one. Stool softeners may cause mild side effects, including stomach or intestinal cramps, upset stomach, or throat irritation (from the oral liquid). If these symptoms are severe or persistent, inform your doctor. Serious side effects, such as skin rash (hives), difficulty breathing or swallowing, fever, vomiting, or stomach pain, require immediate medical attention. If you experience a serious side effect, you or your doctor can report it to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. Store stool softeners in their original container, tightly sealed, and out of reach of children. Keep the medication at room temperature, away from excessive heat and moisture, and do not store it in the bathroom. Dispose of any expired or unused medication properly; consult your pharmacist for guidance on safe disposal. If you have any additional questions about this medication, consult your pharmacist. Common brand names for stool softeners include Colace®, Dialose®, Docusate®, DOS®, Doxinate®, Fleet Sof-Lax®, Hemaspan®, Modane Soft®, and Surfak®.
